_comment: Rotation list for the proactive podcast researcher (scripts/podcast_researcher.py) and the podcast-deep-research workflow (.claude/workflows/podcast-deep-research.js). Each entry is one candidate episode topic. 'domain' defaults to 'medicine'; only medicine topics (with 'pubmed_query' feeding PubMed E-utilities) are eligible for the local PubMed fallback — non-medicine domains ('query' instead) are researched exclusively by the deep-research workflow with domain-appropriate lenses. 'debate' defaults to false (deep dive preferred); set to true only when an explicit adversarial dispute is specifically requested.

topics.title: The A&E Crisis — What's Happening to UK Emergency Departments
topics.query: UK A&E crisis emergency department crowding four hour standard exit block ambulance handover delays causes solutions
topics.angle: Answer four questions, in order, and let the sources rather than the hosts' priors decide each: (1) What is actually happening to UK EDs — the real numbers on four-hour performance, 12-hour DTA waits, ambulance handover delays, bed occupancy, and how they have moved over the last decade. (2) Why — the causal mechanism, distinguishing front-door demand from exit block and whole-system flow, and how much of the change each candidate cause actually accounts for. (3) How to fix it — named interventions with evidence behind them, separated clearly from interventions that are merely asserted, and who would have to act to deliver each. (4) Who is to blame — treat this as a genuine, contested question: lay out each camp's case (underfunding, social-care collapse, workforce attrition, primary-care access, trust-level flow and management, demographic demand, specific political decisions), give each its strongest advocate and its strongest critic, and be willing to conclude that the evidence points harder at some than others rather than distributing blame evenly for the sake of balance.

topics.title: How Daily CRP Trending Became the Norm
topics.pubmed_query: C-reactive protein serial monitoring hospitalized OR repetitive laboratory testing inpatient low value
topics.angle: Investigate how daily serial C-reactive protein (CRP) monitoring evolved from a 1930s laboratory curiosity into hospital medicine's most ubiquitous, entrenched ward ritual. Unpack the historical journey from Oswald Avery's lab discovering pneumococcal C-polysaccharide precipitation to the late-20th-century introduction of cheap, automated turbidimetric autoanalysers that made repeat ordering frictionless. Contrast the biological reality (fixed 19-hour half-life regardless of disease state, 48-hour lag to peak synthesis, and massive biological noise with a within-subject CV of 0.41) with the daily ritual. Explore the cognitive and cultural drivers: the psychological comfort of a single scalar number as a proxy for clinical trajectory ('the fever chart in a test tube'), defensive medico-legal culture, electronic health record (EHR) order sets with automatic repeat checkboxes, and 5am phlebotomy runs. Review the decisive trial evidence—ADAPT-Sepsis (JAMA 2025: 0.09-day difference in antibiotics from daily CRP) and Giannini (2019: daily CRP delayed IV-to-oral switch)—and contrast with where serial CRP genuinely works (biologically timed post-op day 3-5 leak rule-out). Conclude with how hospital systems are successfully using EHR architectural nudges to restore rational biomarker stewardship.

topics.title: Why 'Normal' Saline Is Not Normal
topics.pubmed_query: balanced crystalloid versus saline randomized OR hyperchloremic acidosis 0.9% sodium chloride
topics.angle: Investigate how 0.9% sodium chloride became the default intravenous fluid of every hospital on earth despite matching no body fluid. Trace the history from Latta's 1832 cholera infusions in Leith through Hartog Hamburger's 1896 red-cell haemolysis experiments, which inferred a tonicity for human plasma that later measurement showed was wrong, to the industrial standardisation of the one-litre bag and the word 'normal' printed on it. Contrast the chemistry with the ritual: plasma chloride sits near 100 mmol/L while saline delivers 154, a strong-ion difference of zero that predictably produces hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, renal vasoconstriction and reduced glomerular filtration (Chowdhury 2012, Stewart physiology). Walk through the trial evidence in order and be honest about its size: SMART and SALT-ED (NEJM 2018) as cluster-crossover trials of the ward and ICU default with a roughly one-percentage-point absolute difference in major adverse kidney events; BaSICS (JAMA 2021) and PLUS (NEJM 2022) showing no mortality difference; and the Hammond 2022 meta-analysis putting a high probability on a small benefit from balanced solutions. Give saline its genuine indications — traumatic brain injury and raised intracranial pressure, hypochloraemic alkalosis from vomiting, hyponatraemia, drug compatibility — and ask why, if the evidence favours balanced crystalloids as the default, the bag in the ED still says normal. Conclude with what actually moved prescribing: changing the default fluid in the order set rather than lecturing prescribers.

topics.title: Adrenaline in Cardiac Arrest — Sixty Years on a Dog Study
topics.pubmed_query: epinephrine out-of-hospital cardiac arrest randomized placebo neurological outcome
topics.angle: Investigate how one milligram of adrenaline every three to five minutes became the central drug of advanced life support and stayed there for sixty years. Start with Crile and Dolley's 1906 canine experiments and Redding and Pearson's 1963 dog asphyxial-arrest studies that put adrenaline into resuscitation, and explain how a dose scaled from dogs and the ampoule size was never titrated in humans. Contrast the pharmacology with the goal: alpha-mediated vasoconstriction raises aortic diastolic and coronary perfusion pressure and does produce return of spontaneous circulation, while beta effects raise myocardial oxygen demand, drive arrhythmias, and constrict cerebral microvasculature, so the drug that restarts the heart may be damaging the brain the patient needs to survive with. Walk through the evidence honestly: Olasveengen 2009 and Jacobs 2011 as the underpowered warnings, then PARAMEDIC2 (NEJM 2018, 8,014 patients) with 30-day survival of 3.2% versus 2.4% but no improvement in survival with a favourable neurological outcome and nearly twice the rate of severe neurological impairment among survivors, plus the high-dose adrenaline trials that found nothing. Examine the honest exceptions — non-shockable and asphyxial rhythms, early administration where benefit is largest — and the alternatives that have been tried (vasopressin, vasopressin with steroids). Ask why ILCOR still recommends the drug, what an ROSC-centred versus a neurologically-intact-survival-centred outcome does to the answer, and what a patient or family would choose if told the trade-off plainly.

topics.title: 'Finish the Course' — Where Antibiotic Durations Actually Came From
topics.pubmed_query: antibiotic course duration short versus long randomized OR complete the course resistance
topics.angle: Investigate how fixed antibiotic durations of seven, ten and fourteen days became a public-health commandment and a prescribing reflex when no pharmacology ever produced those numbers. Trace the origin to Fleming's 1945 Nobel lecture and its parable of under-dosed 'Mr X' seeding resistant streptococci, the ten-day penicillin course that came from rheumatic-fever prevention in the 1950s and was generalised to everything, and the observation that durations cluster on multiples of the seven-day week (Llewelyn, BMJ 2017). Contrast the folk theory with the biology: resistance is selected mainly in commensal flora and scales with total exposure, so for most infections longer courses increase rather than reduce the resistance risk, and there is no mechanism by which stopping a course early breeds resistance in the pathogen being treated. Walk through the shorter-is-better trial literature: community-acquired pneumonia at three to five days (el Moussaoui 2006, Uranga 2016), intra-abdominal infection in STOP-IT (NEJM 2015), pyelonephritis at seven days, cellulitis at five days, ventilator-associated pneumonia at eight days, and Gram-negative bacteraemia at seven days in Yahav 2019 and BALANCE (NEJM 2024, 3,608 patients). Give the genuine exceptions their due — tuberculosis, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia, prosthetic material — where duration is load-bearing. Examine the public-messaging tension: patient leaflets and the pharmacy label still say finish the course while the evidence says stop when you are better, and explore how clinicians and health systems can move to indication-specific, patient-responsive durations without undermining adherence messaging where it matters.

topics.title: Nil by Mouth from Midnight — The Fasting Ritual
topics.pubmed_query: preoperative fasting clear fluids aspiration OR procedural sedation fasting emergency department
topics.angle: Investigate how 'nil by mouth from midnight' became a universal instruction for anyone who might have a procedure, and why patients routinely fast for twelve to sixteen hours when the guidance says two. Trace the origin to Mendelson's 1946 series of aspiration in obstetric ether anaesthesia and his rabbit experiments, and to the 25 mL / pH 2.5 gastric-risk threshold derived from a single rhesus monkey (Roberts and Shirley 1974) that shaped policy for forty years. Contrast the ritual with gastric physiology: clear fluids empty with a half-time of ten to twenty minutes and are gone within two hours, which is why the ASA, the Royal College of Anaesthetists and European guidance have allowed clear fluids until two hours before anaesthesia since 1999, with paediatric guidance now at one hour. Show the harms of the ritual — thirst, dehydration, hypotension on induction, hypoglycaemia, delirium in older hip-fracture patients, and cancellations that reset the clock — and the Sip Til Send movement that lets patients drink water until called. Then bring it to the ED: ACEP clinical policy finds no relationship between fasting time and aspiration in procedural sedation, and Bhatt 2018 (JAMA Pediatrics, 6,183 children) found no association either, yet departments still delay sedation for a fasting window. Give the genuine full stomach its due — trauma, opioids, bowel obstruction, gastroparesis, pregnancy — and present gastric point-of-care ultrasound as the rational replacement for the clock. Conclude with why the order set default and nursing culture, not the evidence, are what keep the water jug off the bedside table.

topics.title: The Penicillin Allergy Label — A Diagnosis Nobody Made
topics.pubmed_query: penicillin allergy label delabeling direct oral challenge emergency department
topics.angle: Investigate how roughly one in ten patients came to carry a penicillin allergy label when fewer than one in twenty of them is truly allergic, and why the label follows a patient for life without ever being tested. Trace how the labels arise — an amoxicillin rash during a childhood viral illness, a family history, nausea recorded as allergy — and the immunology that makes most of them obsolete: IgE sensitisation wanes in about eighty percent of truly allergic patients within ten years. Explain the historical accident behind the ten-percent cephalosporin cross-reactivity figure, which came from 1960s cephalosporins contaminated with trace penicillin during production, when the real figure for dissimilar side chains is around two percent. Quantify the harm: Blumenthal's cohort work (BMJ 2018) with substantially higher MRSA and Clostridioides difficile rates, higher surgical-site infection odds, longer stays, and more broad-spectrum and second-line antibiotic use. Walk through the delabelling evidence: the PEN-FAST score (JAMA Internal Medicine 2020), PALACE (JAMA Internal Medicine 2023) showing direct oral challenge non-inferior to skin testing in low-risk patients, and ED and inpatient pharmacist-led delabelling programmes. Give the genuine exceptions their weight — severe cutaneous adverse reactions, recent anaphylaxis, organ-involving reactions — where a label is protective and must not be challenged casually. Conclude with the structural fix: an EHR allergy field that distinguishes allergy from intolerance and records severity, and a pathway that makes removing a wrong label as easy as adding one.

topics.title: The Urine Dip in the Confused Older Patient
topics.pubmed_query: asymptomatic bacteriuria delirium older adults OR urinary tract infection overdiagnosis nursing home
topics.angle: Investigate how 'confused, query UTI' became a reflex diagnosis in emergency departments and care homes, and why the urine dipstick that anchors it is close to meaningless in older adults. Lay out the epidemiology: asymptomatic bacteriuria in a quarter to half of women in long-term care, near-universal in catheterised patients, and pyuria in most of them, so leucocyte esterase and nitrite have almost no positive predictive value in this population. Examine the claimed delirium link honestly — systematic reviews (Mayne 2019) find no robust evidence that bacteriuria causes acute confusion — and show what the label costs: unnecessary antibiotics, Clostridioides difficile, resistance, and above all the missed real cause of the confusion, whether it is a subdural, a drug, hypoxia, constipation, pain, or sepsis somewhere else. Walk through the guidance that already exists — SIGN 160, NICE NG109, the IDSA 2019 asymptomatic bacteriuria guideline, Choosing Wisely, and the English 'To Dip or Not to Dip' care-home programme that cut antibiotic prescribing substantially — and the trials showing that treating asymptomatic bacteriuria increases recurrence and resistance (Cai 2012) without improving outcomes. Give the genuine indications for screening their due — pregnancy and before urological instrumentation — and be clear about what real urosepsis looks like. Conclude with why removing the dipstick from triage and the 'UTI' checkbox from the admission proforma changes behaviour where teaching has not.

topics.title: Routine Oxygen — How a Drug Became a Comfort Blanket
topics.pubmed_query: supplemental oxygen myocardial infarction normoxemia randomized OR hyperoxia stroke
topics.angle: Investigate how supplemental oxygen became a reflex treatment for chest pain, stroke and 'being unwell' in patients whose saturations were normal, and what the trials found when someone finally tested it. Trace the history from Steele's 1900 use of oxygen for angina to the MONA mnemonic that taught generations of students that oxygen is a treatment for myocardial infarction. Contrast the assumption with the physiology: hyperoxia causes coronary vasoconstriction and reduces coronary blood flow by around a fifth, raises systemic vascular resistance, and generates reactive oxygen species during reperfusion — so oxygen given to a normoxaemic patient with an occluded artery may enlarge the infarct rather than shrink it, a signal first seen in Rawles and Kenmure's 1976 trial. Walk through the modern evidence: AVOID (Circulation 2015) with larger infarcts on cardiac MRI in the oxygen arm, DETO2X-SWEDEHEART (NEJM 2017, 6,629 patients) with no mortality benefit, SO2S (JAMA 2017, 8,003 stroke patients) with no benefit, and the critical-care literature — Oxygen-ICU, ICU-ROX, HOT-ICU, and the IOTA meta-analysis (Lancet 2018) linking liberal oxygen to higher mortality. Give oxygen its genuine indications their full weight: hypoxaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, pneumothorax, cluster headache, pre-oxygenation before intubation, and the conditions where a higher target is right. Explore why the ritual persists — the mask as a visible act of care, the reassurance of a high saturation, the absence of a prescription — and how the BTS target-range approach, prescribing oxygen as a drug with a saturation target, changed practice where it was actually implemented.

topics.title: The Cervical Collar and the Spinal Board — Immobilising Without Evidence
topics.pubmed_query: cervical collar spinal immobilization prehospital evidence harm OR rigid backboard
topics.angle: Investigate how the rigid cervical collar and the long spinal board became universal for every trauma patient with a possible neck injury, and how that happened without a single trial showing benefit. Trace the origin to 1960s American pre-hospital doctrine, Farrington's 'Death in a Ditch', and ATLS from 1978 onward, which codified full immobilisation as the standard of care worldwide. Contrast the doctrine with the evidence and the biology: Hauswald's 1998 comparison of Malaysia, where nobody was immobilised, with New Mexico, where everybody was, found less neurological disability without immobilisation; cadaver work (Ben-Galim 2010) showed collars distract unstable upper cervical injuries by several millimetres; collars raise intracranial pressure, cause pressure sores within hours, increase aspiration risk and make the airway harder; boards cause pain and pressure injury within thirty minutes and generate imaging to explain the pain they cause. Quantify how rare unstable injury is in the ambulant, alert patient and what NEXUS and the Canadian C-spine rule already tell us. Walk through the retreat: the 2013 Faculty of Pre-Hospital Care consensus, NAEMSP and ACS-COT positions on boards, Scandinavian and Norwegian guidelines, NICE NG41, the rebranding as spinal motion restriction, and the EXIT project (Nutbeam 2022) showing patients who self-extricate move their spines less than when clinicians extricate them. Give the honest exceptions their weight — the obtunded patient, the high-risk mechanism with focal signs — and ask what should replace the collar. Conclude with why a practice with no evidence base took forty years to loosen, and what that says about how emergency care adopts and abandons rituals.

topics.title: Contrast Nephropathy — The Diagnosis That May Not Exist
topics.pubmed_query: contrast induced nephropathy propensity matched OR post-contrast acute kidney injury controls
topics.angle: Investigate how contrast-induced nephropathy became a feared complication that still delays CT scans in emergency departments, and why much of the modern evidence suggests that for intravenous contrast the entity may be largely a statistical artefact. Trace the origin to 1950s to 1970s case series using high-osmolar ionic agents and to a definition — a creatinine rise of 25% or 0.5 mg/dL within 72 hours — that was never tested against a control group. Show the biological-noise problem first: Newhouse 2008 found that hospitalised patients who received no contrast met the 'nephropathy' definition at rates similar to those who did, because creatinine fluctuates day to day for reasons unrelated to contrast. Walk through the propensity-matched era: McDonald 2013 and 2014 (Radiology) and Hinson 2017 (Annals of Emergency Medicine, 17,934 ED patients) found no excess acute kidney injury, dialysis or death with intravenous contrast; Aycock's 2018 meta-analysis of 28 studies found the same; Davenport 2013 found a signal only below an eGFR of 30; and AMACING (Lancet 2017) and PRESERVE (NEJM 2018) showed prophylactic hydration, bicarbonate and N-acetylcysteine do nothing. Be honest about the genuine residual uncertainty — eGFR below 30, high-volume intra-arterial contrast in cardiology, the observational nature of the reassurance — and about the ACR-NKF 2020 consensus position that contrast should not be withheld when the scan is needed. Quantify what the fear costs: unenhanced or delayed CT pulmonary angiograms, missed diagnoses, hours waiting for a creatinine, metformin holds. Conclude with the joint radiology and emergency medicine guidance and the departmental changes — point-of-care creatinine, removing the creatinine gate — that let the scan happen.

topics.title: Two Sets of Blood Cultures for Everyone
topics.pubmed_query: blood culture yield emergency department cellulitis pneumonia contamination low value
topics.angle: Investigate how drawing two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics became a reflex for every infection, including the ones where they almost never grow anything, and what the reflex costs. Trace the origin to the Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundles and quality metrics such as SEP-1 that made 'cultures before antibiotics' a measured behaviour, which then spread from septic shock to cellulitis, uncomplicated pneumonia and pyelonephritis. Lay out the yield data: bacteraemia in around two percent of cellulitis (Perl 1999), blood cultures changing management in well under one percent of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia (Campbell 2003, IDSA/ATS 2019 guidance against routine culture in non-severe inpatients), and urine cultures making blood cultures redundant in pyelonephritis. Set that against the contamination rate of two to three percent, which in low-prevalence populations means a positive result is more often a contaminant than a true bacteraemia, and quantify the downstream harm — extra vancomycin, extra days in hospital, repeat cultures, and several thousand pounds per false positive. Use Coburn's 2012 JAMA Rational Clinical Examination and the Shapiro decision rule to show who actually needs cultures, and give the genuine indications their full weight: undifferentiated sepsis, suspected endocarditis, Staphylococcus aureus, immunocompromise, indwelling devices, febrile neutropenia, and the fact that culture sensitivity falls substantially once antibiotics have started (Cheng 2019), so when a culture matters it must be drawn first. Walk through diagnostic stewardship programmes (Fabre 2020; Woods-Hill's paediatric ICU work) that cut culture volumes by a third without missing bacteraemia. Conclude with why removing the culture line from the cellulitis and pneumonia order sets works where teaching the yield data has not.

topics.title: A PPI on Every Drug Chart — Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis Beyond the ICU
topics.pubmed_query: stress ulcer prophylaxis proton pump inhibitor randomized ICU OR hospitalized patients overuse
topics.angle: Investigate how stress ulcer prophylaxis, a treatment developed for ventilated intensive-care patients, ended up on the drug chart of most medical and surgical inpatients with no risk factors at all. Trace the origin to Skillman's 1969 description of stress ulceration in critically ill patients and Cook's 1994 NEJM risk-factor study, which identified mechanical ventilation over 48 hours and coagulopathy as the real predictors, and show how the indication then leaked to the general ward until audits found around seventy percent of inpatient prophylaxis inappropriate (Heidelbaugh 2006) and sixty percent of it continued at discharge. Contrast the ward reality with the evidence: SUP-ICU (NEJM 2018, 3,298 patients) with no mortality difference, PEPTIC (JAMA 2020, 26,982 patients) comparing PPI with H2 blockers, and REVISE (NEJM 2024, 4,821 ventilated patients) showing pantoprazole does reduce clinically important upper GI bleeding from 3.5% to 1.0% in the population it was designed for — the honest exception that makes the point, because that population is not the ward patient. Quantify the harms of indiscriminate use: Clostridioides difficile, hospital-acquired pneumonia (Herzig 2009), hypomagnesaemia, fractures and long-term dependence created by a drug started for no reason. Walk through the SCCM 2024 guideline and Choosing Wisely recommendations, and conclude with why the admission order-set default and discharge medicines reconciliation, not prescriber education, are where the ritual is actually broken.

topics.title: 37 Degrees — The Normal Temperature That Isn't
topics.pubmed_query: normal body temperature 37 Wunderlich OR fever control sepsis randomized acetaminophen
topics.angle: Investigate how 37 degrees Celsius became the normal human temperature and 38 the definition of fever, and what it costs to run a hospital on a number from 1868. Trace the origin to Carl Wunderlich's million axillary readings on 25,000 patients using a foot-long thermometer that took twenty minutes to equilibrate, and show what modern measurement found: Mackowiak's 1992 JAMA study putting the mean at 36.8 with an upper limit near 37.7 and a half-degree diurnal swing, and Protsiv's 2020 eLife analysis showing average temperature has fallen by about 0.03 degrees per decade since the American Civil War to roughly 36.6 today. Explain the consequences of one fixed threshold: older adults run lower baselines so their infections present 'afebrile' and are missed, which is why IDSA defines fever in the elderly as 37.8 or a rise of 1.1 degrees above baseline; measurement site changes the answer by up to a degree; and early-warning scores treat a population statistic as an individual property. Then turn to what we do with a fever once we find it: fever is an evolutionarily conserved host defence, and HEAT (NEJM 2015) found that paracetamol for fever in ICU sepsis made no difference to ICU-free days or mortality, while Schulman 2005 was stopped early for a trend toward harm with aggressive fever control in trauma patients. Examine fever phobia in parents and clinicians and the reflex paracetamol that treats the number rather than the patient. Give the genuine exceptions full weight — brain injury and post-cardiac-arrest care where fever avoidance matters, heatstroke where cooling is mandatory, and the unwell patient whose comfort improves. Conclude with what a rational temperature policy would look like: individual baselines, site-specific thresholds, and treating fever for comfort rather than as a target.
